title: Inductive Reasoning for Temporal Knowledge Graphs with Emerging Entities
one_liner: When new entities arrive with no history, borrow the reasoning patterns from similar old entities to predict their future interactions.
lead: Temporal knowledge graphs are like a giant filing cabinet: who talked to whom, and when. When a new person joins, they have no history yet. Existing methods fail because they have never seen this person before. But here is the insight: if the new person is similar to someone already in the cabinet (perhaps they work in the same field, or share the same interests), then they probably behave in similar ways. TransFIR uses this similarity to copy reasoning patterns from known entities to new ones, predicting their interactions even on day one.

paras: A temporal knowledge graph is a recording of interactions over time: which entities (people, companies, events) interacted with which others, and when. The system learns to predict missing or future interactions by studying past patterns.

The problem: new entities arrive all the time, and they have zero history. A person joins a social network today. A business starts up today. The existing reasoning method has nothing to learn from, so it fails catastrophically—accuracy plummets because there are no past interactions to analyze.

callout.html: New entities with no history can borrow reasoning patterns from similar old entities.

steps.text: Compute how similar the new entity is to each known entity using their semantic properties (what field they work in, what they like, who they are).
Rank known entities by similarity. The top few are the candidates to copy from.
For each closest match, retrieve their temporal interaction patterns: who they usually interact with, in what order, at what times.
Blend the patterns from the top similar entities (give more weight to the closer ones) into a composite reasoning rule for the new entity.
Apply this blended pattern to predict who the new entity will interact with next.

paras: Standard temporal knowledge graph reasoning takes one sequence: the interaction history of one entity, and learns patterns from it. When a new entity arrives, there is no sequence to learn from, so the system has no input.

TransFIR changes which sequences the reasoning algorithm uses. Instead of only the new entity's own (empty) history, it also uses the histories of similar known entities. This gives the reasoner actual data to work with.

hidden.h2: Semantic similarity: which entities are cousins
hidden.name: Semantic similarity score
paras: The hidden quantity is a number that measures how much two entities are alike in their inherent properties (not in who they interact with, but in what they are). If both entities are lawyers, or both work in finance, or both are universities in the same region, their similarity score is high.

The paper computes this similarity using a semantic clustering method: a codebook (a short list of standard templates or semantic archetypes) classifies each entity into a latent cluster (a group of 'types'). Entities in the same cluster have high similarity. This clustering is trained once on the known entities, then applied to new arrivals. The paper then uses the cluster assignment to decide which known entities are most similar to the newcomer.

heat.caption: Darker means higher semantic similarity. Frank (new) and Charlie (known) both dark: they are similar types.

reads.html: Semantic similarity is a number that answers: do these two entities have the same nature? Are they both in the same field, region, or type? If yes, they are probably cousins.

The paper uses a learned codebook classifier (trained on known entities) to assign each entity to a latent semantic cluster. Entities in the same cluster are treated as similar and can transfer patterns to each other.

paras: Here is the causal chain: If a new entity is semantically similar to a known entity, they share the same underlying behavioral rules. Lawyers interact with judges and clients in a predictable order and timing. Accountants interact with their clients in a different, but equally stable, pattern. Similarity in nature means similarity in behavior.

When we give the reasoner the known entity's history instead of just the new entity's empty history, the reasoner has real data to learn from. It extracts the temporal patterns (the sequence of interactions, the timing, the types of partners). The new entity can then use those same patterns, because it is the same type.

Why 28.6 percent better? Because with no history, the old method is guessing blindly. With borrowed history, the new method has a solid starting point. The new entity's reasoning becomes as reliable as an established entity's from day one, instead of starting from zero.

stages.s: Measure semantic similarity to known entities
Retrieve top similar entities' interaction histories
Extract temporal patterns from their sequences
Apply patterns to predict new entity's interactions

math.words: For a new entity, compute a weighted average of known entities' interaction patterns, weighted by their semantic similarity to the new entity.
math.equation: pattern(new) = sum_i ( similarity(new, entity_i) * pattern(entity_i) ) / sum_i similarity(new, entity_i)
symbols: the reasoning rules for the new entity
how much the new entity resembles entity i (a number between 0 and 1)
the learned temporal interaction sequence of known entity i
add up over all known entities

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Three known entities (Alice, Bob, Charlie) with similarity scores to new entity Frank: Alice=0.3, Bob=0.5, Charlie=0.9.
Charlie's pattern: interact-with-lawyer, then-colleague, then-repeat. (Charlie is a lawyer, like Frank.)
Weighted pattern for Frank: 0.3*Alice + 0.5*Bob + 0.9*Charlie, divided by (0.3+0.5+0.9=1.7) = 0.18*Alice + 0.29*Bob + 0.53*Charlie.
Charlie dominates (0.53), so Frank's predicted pattern is heavily biased toward Charlie's lawyer behavior.

math.note: The equation weights each known entity's pattern by how similar it is to the newcomer, then blends them. The most similar entities have the loudest voice.

charts.title: Old method (no history transfer)
charts.note: Known entities work fine. New entities crash because the method has no history to learn from.

charts.title: TransFIR (borrows from similar entities)
charts.note: New entities improve 28.6 percent (18 to 46 in this illustrative example), because the method now has actual historical data to extract patterns from instead of an empty record.

items.html: If the similarity score is computed badly (e.g., measuring interactions instead of inherent type), then similar entities may not share behavioral patterns, and predictions fail.
If the new entity is so different from all known entities that no similarity cluster matches, there is no suitable pattern to borrow. The method defaults to random prediction.
If the temporal patterns of similar entities drift or change (because their field or role shifted), then copying an old pattern leads to stale predictions.
If the semantic clustering is trained well (so that true similar entities end up in the same cluster), then the pattern transfer works reliably, even for very new entities.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a tiny temporal knowledge graph: five known entities, each with a short interaction history (a sequence of 5 to 10 interactions over 5 time steps). Train the similarity measure (the codebook classifier) on these five entities. Then introduce two new entities (with no history). For each new entity, measure how similar it is to each of the five known entities using the trained classifier. Retrieve the pattern from the most similar known entity. Use that pattern to predict the new entity's next interaction. Measure accuracy: did the prediction match ground truth?
demo.metric_eq: accuracy = (number of correct predictions on new entities) / (number of new entities) * 100 percent
demo.closing: The demo should make it impossible to miss: new entities, which have zero history and would normally fail, suddenly have reasonable predictions because they borrowed patterns from their closest neighbors.
